summary.text: The Taylor-sum difference is rewritten as \(\beta(pS,pN)-\beta(S,N)\), where \(\beta(S,N)=[X^N]\frac{1-2X}{(1-X)(1-X+X^2)}(1-X)^{-S}\); expanding \(X^p+(1-X)^p=1+ph\) and using a Cartier coefficient identity gives a double sum whose two lowest Stirling-degree parts vanish, the second by antisymmetry under \(X\mapsto1-X\). Kummer and Legendre bounds, Stirling-number valuation estimates, and a product identity for the remaining Stirling sum show that every surviving term has valuation at least \(3(v+1)\) when \(p^v\mid S,N\), and taking \(v=k-1\) and \(S=(m+1)np^{k-1}\) yields the result.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}=1+x+2x^2+5x^3+\cdots
\]
be the Catalan power series.  We prove a slightly more general result, from which the assertion for A333096 is obtained by putting \(m=4\).

Throughout, for \(z\in\mathbb Z\) and \(r\geq0\), write
\[
 {z\choose r}=\frac{z(z-1)\cdots(z-r+1)}{r!}.
\]
This is an integer.  We also use the multichoose notation
\[
 \left(\!\!{z\choose r}\!\!\right)={z+r-1\choose r}.
\]
The usual reflection formula is
\[
 {-z\choose r}=(-1)^r\left(\!\!{z\choose r}\!\!\right).                 \tag{1}
\]
The elementary absorption identities
\[
 (r+1){z\choose r+1}=(z-r){z\choose r},\qquad
 (r+1){z\choose r+1}=z{z-1\choose r}                                  \tag{2}
\]
will be used repeatedly.

For positive \(n\), define
\[
 A_m(n)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\frac{mn}{mn+r}{mn+2r-1\choose r},                \tag{3}
\]
with the summand interpreted by the corresponding integral Catalan coefficient (and with the exceptional zero-denominator expression taken as in the integral formula below). For \(m=4\) no denominator vanishes. Lagrange inversion applied to \(C=1+xC^2\) gives
\[
 [x^r]C(x)^R=\frac{R}{R+r}{R+2r-1\choose r}                            \tag{4}
\]
for positive \(R\). Hence
\[
 A_4(n)=\sum_{r=0}^n[x^r]C(x)^{4n},
\]
which is exactly the value at \(x=1\) of the degree-\(n\) Taylor truncation in the question.

We shall prove, for every integer \(m\), every prime \(p\ge5\), and positive \(N\) divisible by \(p^v\), the one-step congruence
\[
 A_m(pN)\equiv A_m(N)\pmod {p^{3(v+1)}}.                               \tag{5}
\]
Taking \(N=np^{k-1}\) and \(v=k-1\) proves the desired result.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Rewriting the sequence as one coefficient
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Put
\[
 P_0(R)=1,
\]
and, for \(r\ge1\),
\[
 P_r(R)={R+2r-1\choose r}-{R+2r-1\choose r-1}.                         \tag{6}
\]
Identity (2) gives
\[
 R{R+2r-1\choose r}=(R+r)P_r(R).                                      \tag{7}
\]
Thus the summand in (3) equals \(P_r(mn)\), except in the sole singular situation \(m=-1,r=n\). In that situation the convention in (3) gives zero whereas \(P_n(-n)=-1\). Consequently, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
 A_m(n)=\sum_{r=0}^nP_r(mn)+\begin{cases}1,&m=-1,\\0,&m\ne-1.\end{cases} \tag{8}
\]
The exceptional correction is independent of \(n\), so it disappears from every difference \(A_m(n_1)-A_m(n_2)\).

Define the power series
\[
 G(X)=\frac{1-2X}{(1-X)(1-X+X^2)}                                     \tag{9}
\]
and
\[
 \beta(S,N)=[X^N]G(X)(1-X)^{-S}.                                      \tag{10}
\]
We next show
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^N P_r(R)=\beta(R+N,N).                                    \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, using (1), (6), and Pascal's identity, one checks
\[
 P_r(R)=[X^r](1-2X)(1-X)^{-(R+r+1)}.                                  \tag{12}
\]
Set \(Y=X(1-X)\). Since \(1-X+X^2=1-Y\), the finite geometric identity
\[
 \frac1{1-Y}=\sum_{t=0}^NY^t+\frac{Y^{N+1}}{1-Y}
\]
shows that the coefficient of degree \(N\) in
\[
 \frac{1-2X}{(1-X)(1-X+X^2)}(1-X)^{-(R+N)}

a
\]
(the displayed stray “a” is to be ignored; the expression ends after the preceding product)
is the sum, over \(0\le t\le N\), of the degree-\(N\) coefficients of
\[
 (1-2X)(1-X)^{-(R+N+1)}X^t(1-X)^t.
\]
The latter is \(P_{N-t}(R)\) by (12), while the remainder containing \(Y^{N+1}\) has no term of degree \(N\). This proves (11).

Combining (8) and (11), for positive \(n_1,n_2\),
\[
 A_m(n_1)-A_m(n_2)
 =\beta((m+1)n_1,n_1)-\beta((m+1)n_2,n_2).                             \tag{13}
\]
Thus it remains to prove a supercongruence for \(\beta\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. A Cartier fixed-point identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let
\[
 Q(X)=1-X+X^2.
\]
Define the period-six sequence
\[
 e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4,e_5,\ldots=2,1,-1,-2,-1,1,\ldots .
\]
It satisfies \(e_{r+2}=e_{r+1}-e_r\). Therefore
\[
 E(X):=\sum_{r\ge0}e_rX^r=\frac{2-X}{Q(X)}.
\]
Since \((1-X)^{-1}=\sum_{r\ge0}X^r\), equation (9) can be written
\[
 G(X)=E(X)-(1-X)^{-1}.                                                  \tag{14}
\]
In particular, if \(g_r=[X^r]G\), then
\[
 g_r=e_r-1.                                                            \tag{15}
\]

For a prime \(p\ge5\), put
\[
 \Delta(X)=X^p+(1-X)^p.                                                \tag{16}
\]
We claim the Cartier fixed-point formula
\[
 [X^{pj}]\Delta(X)^jG(X)=g_j.                                         \tag{17}
\]
To prove it, expand \(\Delta^j\). Moving the powers of \(X^p\) into the coefficient index gives
\[
 [X^{pj}]\Delta^jF
 =\sum_{K=0}^j{j\choose K}[X^{pK}](1-X)^{pK}F                         \tag{18}
\]
for every power series \(F\).

Two elementary binomial-sum computations now suffice. First,
\[
 [X^M](1-X)^ME(X)=e_{2M}.                                              \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, the left side is
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^M(-1)^{M+a}{M\choose a}e_a,
\]
after reflecting the summation index. Induction on \(M\), using Pascal's identity and \(e_{r+2}=e_{r+1}-e_r\), shows more generally that
\[
 \sum_{a=0}^M(-1)^{M+a}{M\choose a}e_{a+r}=e_{2M+r}.
\]
Second,
\[
 \sum_{K=0}^j{j\choose K}e_{2K+r}=e_{j+r},                             \tag{20}
\]
again by induction on \(j\) and the same recurrence.

Because \(p\ne3\), multiplication by \(p\) does not change whether an integer is divisible by \(3\). Inspection of the period-six sequence therefore gives
\[
 e_{2pK}=e_{2K}.                                                       \tag{21}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
 [X^M](1-X)^M(1-X)^{-1}=0\quad(M\ge1),                                \tag{22}
\]
whereas for \(M=0\) the coefficient is \(1\). Substituting (14), (19), (21), and (22) into (18), and then using (20), yields
\[
 [X^{pj}]\Delta^jG=\sum_{K=0}^j{j\choose K}e_{2K}-1=e_j-1=g_j,
\]
which is (17).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The polynomials governing the error
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Since \(p\) is prime,
\[
 h(X):=\frac{\Delta(X)-1}{p}
      =\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}(-1)^r\frac{{p\choose r}}pX^r                  \tag{23}
\]
has integral coefficients and degree at most \(p-1\). Thus
\[
 \Delta=1+ph.                                                         \tag{24}
\]

A crucial extra factorization is
\[
 h(X)=(1-X)Q(X)\eta(X),                                                \tag{25}
\]
for some \(\eta\in\mathbb Z[X]\), with
\[
 \deg\eta\le p-4,
 \qquad \eta(0)=0.                                                     \tag{26}
\]
Here is the proof. Since a prime \(p\ge5\) is congruent to \(1\) or \(5\pmod6\), and since \(Q\) divides both \(X^6-1\) and \((1-X)^6-1\), direct reduction modulo \(Q\) gives
\[
 Q\mid X^p+(1-X)^p-1=\Delta-1.
\]
For the residue class \(5\pmod6\), one also uses the direct identity
\[
 Q\mid X^5+(1-X)^5-1.
\]
Because \(Q\) is monic, (23) implies \(Q\mid h\). Also \(h(1)=0\), so \(1-X\mid h/Q\), proving (25). The degree bound follows from \(\deg h\le p-1\), and \(\eta(0)=0\) follows by evaluating (25) at zero, since \(h(0)=0\) and \(Q(0)=1\).

Put
\[
 \psi(X)=\eta(X)(1-2X),\qquad
 \pi_i(X)=\psi(X)h(X)^{i-1}\quad(i\ge1).                              \tag{27}
\]
By (9) and (25),
\[
 h(X)G(X)=\psi(X),
\]
and hence
\[
 h(X)^iG(X)=\pi_i(X).                                                  \tag{28}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \pi_i(0)=0,
 \qquad \deg\pi_i\le i(p-1)-2.                                      \tag{29}
\]

We need one further cancellation property. Let \(s(a,c)\) denote the signed Stirling number of the first kind, defined by
\[
 T(T-1)\cdots(T-a+1)=\sum_c s(a,c)T^c.
\]
For an integral polynomial \(\pi=\sum_a\pi_aX^a\), define
\[
 U_c(\pi)=\sum_a\frac{(-1)^a\pi_a s(a,c)}{a!}\in\mathbb Q.            \tag{30}
\]
Then
\[
 U_0(\pi_i)=U_1(\pi_i)=0.                                             \tag{31}
\]
The first equality follows immediately from \(\pi_i(0)=0\), because \(s(a,0)=0\) for \(a>0\).

For the second, observe that \(\Delta(1-X)=\Delta(X)\), hence \(h(1-X)=h(X)\). From (25) one obtains
\[
 X\eta(1-X)=(1-X)\eta(X).
\]
Since \(1-2(1-X)=-(1-2X)\), equation (27) implies
\[
 X\pi_i(1-X)=-(1-X)\pi_i(X).
\]
As \(\pi_i(0)=0\), write \(\pi_i=Xq_i\); cancellation gives
\[
 q_i(1-X)=-q_i(X).                                                     \tag{32}
\]
Now \(s(a,1)=(-1)^{a-1}(a-1)!\) for \(a\ge1\). Therefore
\[
 U_1(\pi_i)=-\sum_{b\ge0}\frac{[X^b]q_i(X)}{b+1}.                    \tag{33}
\]
The sum on the right is \(\int_0^1q_i(x)\,dx\), which is zero by the change of variable \(x\mapsto1-x\) and (32). This proves (31).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The master identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(S\in\mathbb Z\) and \(N\ge1\). Define the Stirling numbers of the second kind by
\[
 \left\{\!{0\atop0}\!\right\}=1,
 \qquad
 \left\{\!{c+1\atop j+1}\!\right\}
 =(j+1)\left\{\!{c\atop j+1}\!\right\}
  +\left\{\!{c\atop j}\!\right\}.
\]
They satisfy
\[
 K^c=\sum_j\left\{\!{c\atop j}\!\right\}j!{K\choose j}           \tag{34}
\]
and therefore, by binomial inversion,
\[
 \sum_{K=0}^j{j\choose K}(-1)^KK^c
 =(-1)^jj!\left\{\!{c\atop j}\!\right\}.                           \tag{35}
\]
Define
\[
 \Xi_c(S,N)=
 \sum_{j=1}^{\min(c,N)}(-1)^jj!
 \left\{\!{c\atop j}\!\right\}
 \left(\!\!{S\choose N-j}\!\!\right).                              \tag{36}
\]

We claim the following exact identity in \(\mathbb Q\):
\[
\begin{split}
 \beta(pS,pN)-\beta(S,N)
   =\sum_{i=1}^{pN}\sum_{c=2}^{pN(p-1)}
 &{-S-N\choose i}\,p^{i+c}\,U_c(\pi_i)\,\Xi_c(S,N).                 \tag{37}
\end{split}
\]
We now derive it.

First, decompose
\[
 (1-X)^p=\Delta-X^p
       =\Delta\left(1-X^p\Delta^{-1}\right).                          \tag{38}
\]
Expanding the second factor by the generalized binomial theorem, and extracting degree \(pN\), gives
\[
 \beta(pS,pN)=
 \sum_{j=0}^N
 \left(\!\!{S\choose N-j}\!\!\right)
 [X^{pj}]G(X)\Delta(X)^{j-S-N}.                                       \tag{39}
\]
Indeed, the term indexed by \(N-j\) contributes \(X^{p(N-j)}\), leaving degree \(pj\), and its remaining power of \(\Delta\) is exactly \(j-S-N\).

Using \(\Delta=1+ph\), expand the coefficient in (39):
\[
\begin{split}
 [X^{pj}]G\Delta^{j-S-N}
  &=[X^{pj}]G\Delta^j(1+ph)^{-S-N}\\
  &=g_j+\sum_{i=1}^{pN}{-S-N\choose i}p^iC_{ij},                     \tag{40}
\end{split}
\]
where
\[
 C_{ij}=[X^{pj}]\Delta^j h^iG=[X^{pj}]\Delta^j\pi_i.                 \tag{41}
\]
The term \(i=0\) is \(g_j\) by (17). Terms with \(i>pN\) cannot contribute because \(h(0)=0\). On the other hand, direct convolution in (10) and (15) gives
\[
 \beta(S,N)=\sum_{j=0}^N
 \left(\!\!{S\choose N-j}\!\!\right)g_j.                           \tag{42}
\]
Subtracting (42) from (39) with (40) leaves a double sum involving \(C_{ij}\).

To expand \(C_{ij}\), first use (18), now with \(F=\pi_i\):
\[
 C_{ij}=\sum_{K=0}^j{j\choose K}(-1)^KF(\pi_i,pK),                   \tag{43}
\]
where
\[
 F(\pi,M)=\sum_a(-1)^a\pi_a{M\choose a}.                             \tag{44}
\]
(The sign in (43) follows because \(p\) is odd.) Expanding the falling factorial in powers gives
\[
 {M\choose a}=\frac1{a!}\sum_c s(a,c)M^c,
\]
so (30) and (44) imply
\[
 F(\pi,M)=\sum_cU_c(\pi)M^c.                                         \tag{45}
\]
Substitute (45) into (43), interchange the finite sums, and use (35). This yields
\[
 C_{ij}=\sum_c U_c(\pi_i)p^c(-1)^jj!
 \left\{\!{c\atop j}\!\right\}.                                  \tag{46}
\]
The range may be truncated at \(c=pN(p-1)\) by (29). The terms \(c=0,1\) vanish by (31). Finally, substituting (46) in the difference obtained from (39)–(42), interchanging the \(j,i,c\) sums, and recognizing (36), proves (37).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Valuation estimates
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write \(\nu(r)=v_p(r)\) for the \(p\)-adic order of a nonzero integer, and extend it to rational numbers in the usual way; statements below involving zero are automatic. We collect the estimates needed for each summand of (37).

First, if \(p^v\mid M\) and \(i\ge1\), then
\[
 v_p{-M\choose i}\ge v-\min(v,\nu(i)).                               \tag{47}
\]
One proof follows directly from the second identity in (2):
\[
 i{-M\choose i}=(-M){-M-1\choose i-1}.
\]
This gives the lower bound \(v-\nu(i)\); combining it with the fact that the binomial coefficient is integral replaces a negative lower bound by zero and gives (47).

We shall also use the analogous estimate
\[
 v_p{-S\choose K}\ge v-\min(v,\nu(K))\quad(p^v\mid S).               \tag{48}
\]
For completeness, this can alternatively be seen from Kummer's theorem. If \(S<0\), the left side is the valuation of an ordinary binomial coefficient \({-S\choose K}\); if \(S>0\), reflection (1) turns it into the valuation of \({S+K-1\choose K}\); and if \(S=0\), it vanishes for \(K>0\). In either nonzero case, for every
\(
\nu(K)<r\le v
\)
there is a carry in the \(r\)-th base-\(p\) place, because \(p^r\mid S\) but \(p^r\nmid K\). Kummer's theorem therefore supplies at least \(v-\nu(K)\) carries.

Next we need bounds for \(U_c\). If \(\deg\pi+2\le i(p-1)\), Legendre's formula gives
\[
 \nu(a!)\le i-1\qquad(0\le a\le\deg\pi),
\]
and hence directly from (30)
\[
 v_p(U_c(\pi))\ge-(i-1).                                               \tag{49}
\]
A second bound is useful when \(c\) is small. Let \(D\ge\deg\pi\), and let
\[
 L=\lfloor\log_pD\rfloor.
\]
Every \(1\le t\le D\) has \(\nu(t)\le L\). The recurrence
\[
 s(a+1,c+1)=s(a,c)-a\,s(a,c+1)
\]
proves by induction on \(a\) that
\[
 v_p(s(a,c))\ge
 \nu((a-1)!)-\min\bigl(\nu((a-1)!),(c-1)L\bigr).                     \tag{50}
\]
After division by \(a!\), (50), together with \(\nu(a)\le L\), shows term by term in (30) that
\[
 v_p(U_c(\pi))\ge-cL\qquad(c\ge1).                                   \tag{51}
\]
For \(\pi=\pi_i\), we may take
\[
 D=i(p-1)-2,\qquad L=\lfloor\log_p(i(p-1)-2)\rfloor                  \tag{52}
\]
by (29).

We now establish the special estimate for \(\Xi_c\). Define
\[
 P(Y,r)=\prod_{s=1}^r(Y-s)
\]
and
\[
\begin{split}
 f_c(X,Y)=\sum_{j=1}^c&(-1)^{c-j}j!
 \left\{\!{c\atop j}\!\right\}
 \prod_{e=0}^{c-j-1}(X-c+e)
 \prod_{s=1}^{j-1}(Y-s).                                              \tag{53}
\end{split}
\]
Repeated use of (2) gives, when \(c\le N\),
\[
 \Xi_c(S,N)P(N,c-1)
 =(-1)^N{-S\choose N-c}f_c(S+N,N).                                   \tag{54}
\]
This is obtained term by term from (36): multiply the term indexed by \(j\) by \(P(N,c-1)\), split off \(P(N,j-1)\), and use (2) \(c-j\) times to lower the binomial index from \(N-j\) to \(N-c\). The remaining consecutive factors are exactly those in (53).

For \(c\ge2\),
\[
 f_c(0,0)=0.                                                          \tag{55}
\]
Indeed, at \(X=Y=0\), the products in (53) reduce to signed descending factorials, and their common factor is \(c!\). The remaining sum is
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^c(-1)^{j-1}(j-1)!
 \left\{\!{c\atop j}\!\right\}=0.                                  \tag{56}
\]
Equation (56) follows at once by inserting the recurrence for the Stirling numbers of the second kind: after shifting one of the resulting sums, consecutive terms cancel. Thus, if \(p^v\mid S\) and \(p^v\mid N\), (55) implies
\[
 p^v\mid f_c(S+N,N).                                                   \tag{57}
\]

Assume now that \(2\le c<p^v\). Since \(p^v\mid N\), one has
\[
 \nu(N-c)=\nu(c).
\]
By (48),
\[
 v_p{-S\choose N-c}\ge v-\nu(c).                                    \tag{58}
\]
Furthermore, each factor \(N-s\), \(1\le s<c<p^v\), has exactly the same \(p\)-adic order as \(s\). Therefore
\[
 v_p(P(N,c-1))=\nu((c-1)!).                                           \tag{59}
\]
Combining (54), (57), (58), and (59), and using
\(
\nu(c!)=\nu(c)+\nu((c-1)!)
\), gives
\[
 v_p(\Xi_c(S,N))\ge2v-\nu(c!).                                       \tag{60}
\]

Finally, because \(p\ge5\), Legendre's formula gives the convenient estimate
\[
 4\nu(c!)\le c-1.                                                      \tag{61}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Termwise estimate in the master identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume \(p^v\mid S\), \(p^v\mid N\), and \(N\ge1\). Fix a term in (37), with \(i\ge1\) and \(c\ge2\), and put
\[
 \mu=\min(v,\nu(i)).
\]
Because \(p^v\mid S+N\), (47) gives valuation at least \(v-\mu\) for the binomial factor, while \(p^{i+c}\) contributes \(i+c\).

We prove that every term has valuation at least \(3(v+1)\). There are three cases.

Case 1: \(c\ge p^v\).

Use the general bound (49) for \(U_c(\pi_i)\), and only integrality for \(\Xi_c\). The total valuation is at least
\[
 (v-\mu)+(i+c)-(i-1)=v+c+1-\mu.                                      \tag{62}
\]
If \(v=0\), this is at least \(c+1\ge3\). If \(v\ge1\), the elementary induction
\[
 3v+2\le5^v\le p^v                                                    \tag{63}
\]
and \(\mu\le v\) show that (62) is at least \(3v+3\).

Case 2: \(c<p^v\) and
\[
 c\ge2+\mu+\nu(c!).                                                    \tag{64}
\]
Use (49) and (60). The total valuation is at least
\[
 (v-\mu)+(i+c)-(i-1)+(2v-\nu(c!))
 =3v+c+1-\mu-\nu(c!),
\]
which is at least \(3v+3\) by (64).

Case 3: \(c<p^v\) and
\[
 c<2+\mu+\nu(c!).                                                      \tag{65}
\]
Here use (51), with \(D,L\) as in (52), together with (60). The total valuation is at least
\[
 3v-\mu+i+c-cL-\nu(c!).                                               \tag{66}
\]
Thus it remains to verify
\[
 3+\mu+cL+\nu(c!)\le i+c.                                             \tag{67}
\]
We include the elementary numerical argument because this is the tight part of the estimate.

From (61) and (65),
\[
 3c\le3+4\mu.                                                         \tag{68}
\]
In particular \(\mu\ge1\), so \(\nu(i)\ge1\), and
\[
 p^{\nu(i)}\le i.                                                      \tag{69}
\]
If \(L\le1\), use \(cL\le c\), (61), (68), \(p\ge5\), (69), and the elementary induction
\[
 16r+39\le12\cdot5^r\qquad(r\ge1)                                   \tag{70}
\]
to obtain (67). Explicitly, (68) bounds both \(c\) and \(4\nu(c!)\) linearly in \(\mu\), while (70) bounds the resulting linear expression by \(5^\mu\le5^{\nu(i)}\le p^{\nu(i)}\le i\).

Suppose now \(L\ge2\), and put \(\ell=\lfloor\log_pi\rfloor\). Since
\[
 i(p-1)-2<p^{\ell+2},
\]
we have \(L\le\ell+1\). If \(\ell<2\), then \(\ell=1\), \(L=2\), and (68) forces \(c=2\) and \(\nu(c!)=0\). Also \(p^2\le i(p-1)-2\), which implies \(i\ge p+2\). Hence
\[
 3+\mu+cL+\nu(c!)\le3+1+4\le i+2=i+c.
\]
If \(\ell\ge2\), use
\[
 16\ell^2+44\ell+24\le12\cdot5^\ell                                \tag{71}
\]
(which follows by induction, the initial case being \(\ell=2\)). Together with
\[
 5^\ell\le p^\ell\le i,
\quad L\le\ell+1,
\quad \mu\le\nu(i)\le\ell,

a
\]
(the displayed stray “a” is again to be ignored)
and (61), (68), inequality (71) gives (67) after multiplication by \(12\) and collection of terms. Thus (67) holds in every subcase, and (66) is at least \(3v+3\).

We have proved that every summand on the right side of (37) has \(p\)-adic valuation at least \(3(v+1)\). A finite sum has at least the minimum valuation of its summands, so
\[
 p^{3(v+1)}\mid \beta(pS,pN)-\beta(S,N).                              \tag{72}
\]
Although (37) was written in \(\mathbb Q\), its left side is an integer; the valuation bound therefore gives the asserted ordinary integer divisibility.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Completion of the proof
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(p\ge5\) be prime and let \(n,k\) be positive. Put
\[
 N=np^{k-1},\qquad v=k-1,
\qquad S=(m+1)N.
\]
Then \(p^v\mid N\) and \(p^v\mid S\). Applying (72) gives
\[
 \beta(pS,pN)\equiv\beta(S,N)\pmod {p^{3k}}.                          \tag{73}
\]
But \(pN=np^k\), and (13) says precisely that the difference in (73) is
\[
 A_m(np^k)-A_m(np^{k-1}).
\]
Therefore
\[
 A_m(np^k)\equiv A_m(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}.                          \tag{74}
\]
Finally take \(m=4\). By (4), \(A_4(r)\) is the value at \(1\) of the degree-\(r\) Taylor truncation of \(C(x)^{4r}\), namely the OEIS sequence A333096. Thus, for every prime \(p\ge5\) and all positive integers \(n,k\),
\[
 \boxed{A333096(np^k)\equiv A333096(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}}.
\]
